newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian interest rates seen having hit bottom.
newsitem.headline: Canadian interest rates seen having hit bottom.

text.p: Signs of a reviving economy along with a weaker currency likely spell the end of a spate of rate-cutting by Canada's central bank that has dropped interest rates to 40-year lows, economists said on Thursday.

"The easing is over" said Andrew Spence, senior economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "I think there's good reason for it. If you look at pretty much any indicator of domestic demand, they (indicators) are moving higher."

The Bank of Canada surprised many in the financial community by lowering Canadian short-term interest rates 11 times this year. The central bank last cut its key rate on Nov. 8 to a 35-year low of 3.25 percent. The bank rate is similar to the U.S. Fed funds rate, which is 5.25 percent.
Canada's commercial banks responded to the central bank cuts by lowering their prime lending rate to 4.75 percent, the lowest since March 1956.

The Bank of Canada cut rates to help spur an economy hobbled by deep government spending cuts and a 10 percent unemployment rate. The high jobless rate has dampened consumer confidence, weakening the economy. Many economists forecast the economy will grow by less than 2 percent in 1996.
But there are signs Canada's economy is strengthening, particularly in interest rate-sensitive sectors.
Housing starts rose a stronger-than-expected 17 percent in November from October. A government report on Thursday showed new motor vehicle sales up 3.7 percent in October from the previous month.
Canada's economy is seen growing by at least 3 percent in 1997.

"There's enough slack in terms of monetary policy right now in the economy to get things going on a sustainable basis over 1997," said John Anania, an economist with Royal Bank of Canada. "We don't see the need for any more interest rate cuts."

The Canadian dollar's recent weakness is the other major factor seen preventing more Bank of Canada cuts. The dollar has lost more than 2 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar since just before the last rate cut on Nov. 8.

"(Monetary) conditions have actually loosened up a lot more in the last month because the dollar has fallen out of bed," said Doug Porter, senior economist with Nesbitt Burns. "Where interest rates go are as much a function of how the dollar performs as much as the economy."

Economists said there was a slim possibility that the Bank of Canada could cut one more time if there was a strong rally in the Canadian dollar. A stronger currency would tighten monetary condtions and have the same impact as an interest rate hike.

"If you get that strength, there's the possibility of one more cut. If you don't get that strength in the currency though, our feeling is the overnight rate may be at the bottom of the cycle here," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist with Bank of Montreal.
Ferley said the currency needed to strengthen to at least C$1.3250 ($0.7547) from the current C$1.3575 ($0.7366) for the bank to consider another cut.
